fields.features_heading: What a Life Coaching Intake Form Should Ask
fields.features_subheading: Six parts that hand the coach a plan for the first session instead of a stack of answers.
fields.feature_1:
Life areas rated on one scale

Ask the client to score career, money, health, relationships, and two more areas out of 10. The two lowest ratings move to the top of the prep sheet you read before the first call.
fields.feature_2:
Goals kept in the client's words

Ask what the client wants changed over the engagement and why now, in free text. The form saves the answer word for word for you to quote back to the client in a later session.
fields.feature_3:
Questions for the program they bought

Show career clients questions about offers and target roles, and business owners questions about revenue and staff. Life coaching clients skip both and go straight to their goals.
fields.feature_4:
A coaching agreement, signed on the form

Close with your agreement: session length, the rescheduling window, confidentiality, and what coaching does not cover. The client signs by typing or drawing, and the copy is saved.
fields.feature_5:
A prep sheet before the first call

Turn each submitted intake into one page for the coach, with the lowest scores and flagged answers on top. An email tells the coach when it arrives and names the client.
fields.feature_6:
Source code in your repository

Export the intake form and its client database to GitHub on paid plans as source code. Host it yourself, or have a developer add it to the booking page of your coaching website.

fields.usecase_heading: Intake Forms for Four Kinds of Coaching
fields.tab_content_1:
Session one opens on her two lowest scores

Leah Moreno coaches new parents going back to work. Her intake asks each client to rate six areas of life on a 10-point scale and add a line on each. Dana Whitfield gives health a 3 and money a 4. Those two scores head Leah's prep sheet with Dana's notes beside them and set the agenda for the first call.
fields.tab_content_2:
By day 90, the 62-hour weeks are down to 48

Grant Ellison coaches owners of service businesses. His intake asks for five numbers, hours worked a week among them, and on day 90 the same five go out again. Tessa Park runs a cleaning company. She logged 62 hours at intake and 48 at the check-in, and Grant reads both in one table.
fields.tab_content_3:
When an offer ends within 14 days, the coach knows today

Clearpath Careers puts two questions near the top of its intake: whether the client holds a job offer, and when it expires. Jordan Lee answers yes, in nine days. Any deadline under 14 days sends Omar Haddad a direct message with the role and the date, and Jordan is offered a session this week.
fields.tab_content_4:
The sponsor and the executive answer separately

Ruth Akande starts each engagement with an intake for the executive and a shorter one for the company sponsor. At Varrow, Mira Shah in People names three goals for Daniel Kim, who names three of his own. Ruth reads the lists side by side. The goal only Mira named goes on the agenda for the three-way kickoff.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a Life Coaching Intake Form
fields.howto_description: Follow these seven steps to build a life coaching intake form whose answers tell you how to run each client's first session.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Decide what session one is for
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Add a section for each program
fields.howto_step_1_des: Write down what you need to know before the first call and what you will do with each answer. A question whose answer changes nothing about the session belongs in a later check-in, or off the form entirely.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Give each area of life a score instead of a box for a description. A client who writes "stressed" about work tells you less than one who scores career a 4. A number can also be asked again later and compared.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Ask about past coaching and what the client has already tried in a handful of questions. Leave the long life history for conversation. Coaching works forward from where the client is now, and the goals section deserves the client's best attention.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Career clients need questions about offers, deadlines and target roles. Business owners need the figures you plan to track, such as hours worked and monthly revenue. Give each set its own section and show it only to clients of that program.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Paste in your sections and mark the answers you want to hear about the same day. Emergent builds the form with its database and the email alerts. A new program later needs one more prompt describing its section, and the live form shows it.
fields.howto_step_6_des: End with your agreement: fees, session length, the rescheduling window, and what coaching is not. Ask the client to sign before you book the first session. Have a lawyer read the payment and cancellation terms before the first client signs.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Send it after the discovery call
fields.howto_step_7_des: Send the link once the client says yes on the discovery call, a few days before the first session, which leaves time to read every answer. Fill it in once yourself as a test client and check that each alert reaches you.

plan.angle: The live top 10 is printable PDFs, question lists from coaching-software blogs, a Pinterest board and a free-forms page. Every one stops at the questions. This page treats the intake as the prep for session one: what the coach reads before the first call and what changes because of an answer. Four coaching practices show it: a life coach whose two lowest life-area ratings set the first agenda, a business coach who asks the same baseline numbers again at day 90, a career coach who hears the same day about a job offer with a deadline, and an executive coach who reads the sponsor's goals beside the executive's own.

A career coach's intake asks whether the client holds a job offer and when it expires, and any deadline under 14 days sends the coach a direct message the same day.

intent.evidence: Top 10 is question lists and PDFs; page answers the AlsoAsked question verbatim (FAQ 3), defines the form, covers template, free, business, executive and career variants and a 7-step how-to.

specificity.evidence: Six life areas on a 10-point scale, day-90 re-ask of five baseline numbers, 14-day job-offer rule, sponsor vs executive goal lists.

openers.evidence: 'Leah Moreno coaches new parents going back to work.', 'Grant Ellison coaches owners of service businesses.', 'Give each area of life a score instead of a box'.

craft.evidence: QC clean; varied sentence length ('Ruth reads the lists side by side.').

voice.evidence: Concrete, unglamorous detail ('No budget since leave', '62 hours at intake and 48 at the check-in'); notes only.

truth.evidence: Third-party statements sourced (wheel of life, three-way meeting, agreement before coaching, intake after discovery call); claims map to prompt-build, alerts, e-signature-capture, no-caps, free-start, code-export; numbers agree (3 and 4 lowest, 62 to 48, 9 < 14, 2 of 3).

distinct.evidence: Prep-sheet angle distinct from client-onboarding-questionnaire and personal-training-intake-form; absorbed business-coaching keyword used as intended.
